messages.author: d56eae2dfd7b9848
messages.subject: Detection probability and survey timing
parts:
Dear DISTANCErs,



We=92ve just completed line-transect surveys for large ungulates in the
Eastern Plains Landscape of Cambodia. Surveys were timed for the season
(late Jan through May) when visibility (and hence probably detectability of
focal species) is greatest following the burning of the deciduous

dipterocarp forest which removes most of the grass understorey. Despite a
lot of effort (>500-km of >60 transects) the number of encounters of some
focal species is low (e.g. <35 encounters of Banteng and Eurasian Wild Pig)=
.
Therefore we are planning to re-survey all transects once in the 2010/2011
dry-season (an additional 250-km) to increase sample size.
My question regards the timing of these surveys. Is it sensible to begin
these surveys in November, when the sites become accessible after the

wet-season but prior to burning, and therefore visibility/detectability of
focal species may be lower (due to higher grass) or should we wait until
late-Jan to coincide the timing surveys with those from the 2009/10? If
detection varies between surveys is this likely to be a major problem in th=

e
analysis (intuitively it would seem to be so but some advice would be
appreciated)



Thanks



Tom Gray

--=20
Dr Thomas Gray
Biodiversity research technical adviser
Eastern Plains Landscape Project
WWF Cambodia

messages.author: 12f269733c6eb9a2
messages.subject: Re: Detection probability and survey timing
parts:
Tom:

By changing the timing of your survey you will increase the likelihood=20
that your detection function will differ between surveys; but even=20
keeping your surveys consistent just after the burning season does not=20
guarantee you will have constant detection functions.

Note, I am treating the term 'survey' as a period during which you wish=20
to produce an abundance estimate. I'm not certain from the context of=20
your question whether you are contemplating extending the duration of=20
your survey to encompass both the post-burn season as well as the=20
dry-season and merging all of the data collected into a single=20
population estimate. That will be challenging fundamentally from a=20
biological standpoint; over what duration are you willing to assume=20
constancy of the population you are studying?

If on the other hand, you wish to perform a survey during the post-burn=20
period and a second survey during the dry season, and compare your=20
findings, then you need not be concerned about differences in detection=20
functions between surveys because that will be accommodated in your=20
analysis.

Steer me back in the right direction if I have misunderstood your questio=
n.
